analysis.one_liner: Caps western wholesale electricity prices at the utilities' cost of producing power until markets are fair.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past a committee hearing and died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003, so no cost-based price caps were imposed.
analysis.plain_summary: During the western energy crisis, wholesale electricity prices spiked to many times their normal level and FERC itself found them unjust and unreasonable [S3]. This bill, from Sen. Dianne Feinstein with Sen. Barbara Boxer, would have ordered FERC to cap wholesale power prices in eleven western states at the sellers' actual costs plus a reasonable return, and to keep the caps in place until the market delivered fair prices on its own [S2, S3]. It went to the Senate Energy Committee, got one hearing, and never received a vote before the Congress ended [S1, S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Electricity customers in eleven western states—Arizona, California, Colorado, Idaho, Montana, Nevada, New Mexico, Oregon, Utah, Washington, and Wyoming—would have paid wholesale prices tied to the actual cost of generating power rather than crisis-level spot prices, and those costs ultimately flow into household and business electric bills [S2, S3]. California utilities teetering on insolvency from buying expensive power would also have gained relief [S3].

how_it_helps.text: It orders FERC to set wholesale power prices based on what it costs to generate the electricity, plus a reasonable return, rather than letting spot-market prices run to many times their normal levels.
The bill cites FERC's own November 2000 finding that western power prices were unjust and unreasonable, and uses that as the basis for Congress stepping in.
The caps would stay in effect until the market was actually delivering fair rates, as determined by FERC, rather than expiring on a fixed date.

analysis.who_pays: Wholesale power sellers—generators and energy traders—would have had crisis-era profits capped at their costs plus a reasonable return, and sellers argued caps could reduce investment in new power plants [S3].

drawbacks.text: Price caps can discourage investment in new power plants and conservation by guaranteeing sellers only a cost-plus return rather than market prices, and the bill gives FERC wide discretion to decide when the cap comes off.
Setting rates by law overrides the agency's usual case-by-case rate-setting, which critics argued could distort the western market beyond California and last longer than the crisis warranted.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit—hard caps on what electricity sellers could charge wholesale—would have come quickly and directly to consumers, and was aimed at prices FERC itself had already found unlawful. Its costs were real but speculative: price controls can discourage investment in new generation, and a rigid formula could be outmaneuvered by sellers restructuring contracts. Even so, a temporary cap backed by FERC's own "unjust and unreasonable" finding was a defensible emergency response. The deeper problem was not the design but the absence of action: the bill never even got a committee vote, so neither its benefits nor its costs were ever tested.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Energy Committee held one hearing in March 2001 but never voted on the bill, and it died quietly when the Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 8, 2001 and referred to the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, where it stayed.
The committee held hearings on the bill in March 2001, printing them as S.Hrg. 107-49, but took no further action.
No committee vote, no floor vote, and no House action ever occurred; the bill died when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The electricity sellers and traders who were collecting crisis-level wholesale prices were better off, since the cost-based caps were never imposed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wholesale power sellers kept crisis prices

for.name: Sen. Dianne Feinstein
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to impose cost-based caps on western wholesale electricity prices.

for.name: Sen. Barbara Boxer
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor of the bill.

for.name: Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources
for.what_they_did: Held a hearing on the bill in March 2001, its only action beyond referral.

against.name: Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources
against.what_they_did: Held hearings on the bill in March 2001 but never voted it out of committee.

against.name: Wholesale power sellers and energy trading companies
against.role: Generators and traders selling into the western spot market
against.what_they_did: Benefited from unregulated spot prices and opposed cost-based rate caps.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by two California Democrats, and with a 49-49 Senate and Republican leadership controlling the committee calendar, it never moved beyond a hearing; no roll-call vote was ever taken.

industries.industry: Wholesale power sellers and merchant energy traders
industries.note: These sellers were earning prices many times the historical level during the crisis; cost-based rate caps would have stripped those gains back to cost plus a reasonable return. The bill's findings cite FERC's own finding that the prices were unjust and unreasonable.

industries.industry: Public utilities and electricity distribution companies
industries.note: Utilities buying power at wholesale would have paid far less, easing the financial strain that contributed to utility insolvencies in California; the exact effect varies by whether a utility was a net buyer or seller.
The bill would have pushed FERC to use its cost-of-service rate authority aggressively, strengthening rather than weakening the regulator's role over wholesale markets.
